akustik.title: 🎶 The acoustic adventure 🥁
akustik.subtitle: Hello sound master! Get your ears tuned as we immerse ourselves in the invisible and loud world of sound!

sections.title: 1. Origin: Everything shakes!

quizzes.question: What actually creates a sound or a noise?

answers.text: Through a rapid back and forth movement (oscillation).
answers.feedback: Genau: Ohne Schwingung gibt es keinen Ton.

answers.text: Through invisible magic in the air.
answers.feedback: Nicht Magie: Etwas muss schnell hin und her schwingen, zum Beispiel Stimmbänder oder eine Saite.

sections.content:
Regardless of whether you are speaking, clapping your hands or plucking a guitar - sounds are always created by only one thing: Movement! An object shakes back and forth extremely quickly. Physicists call this oscillation. When your vocal cords vibrate in your throat, your voice is created. When you speak, put your hand on your larynx - you can feel the trembling!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Sound Source
The thing that shakes and produces the sound is called sound source. This can be the head of a drum, the string of a violin or the metal sheet of a tuning fork.

sections.title: 2. The medium: The silent emptiness of space

quizzes.question: Why don't you hear outside noises in space in spacesuits?

answers.text: Because the helmets are too thick.
answers.feedback: Der Helm schützt, aber das ist nicht der Hauptgrund. Schall braucht Teilchen zwischen Quelle und Ohr.

answers.text: Because in the vacuum of space there are no air particles that can carry sound.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Im Vakuum fehlen Teilchen, die den Schall weitergeben.

sections.content:
Imagine you are standing on the moon and a huge meteorite crashes silently into the ground. Silent? Yes! In order for the sound from the tuning fork to reach your ear, it needs tiny “postmen”. These are the air particles. The tuning fork pushes the air, the air particles push their neighbors, and so the sound wave travels into your ear.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Vacuum
Sound always needs a substance (a Medium) to propagate. This can be air, but also water or even iron! Where there is absolutely nothing - like in space - it is called Vacuum. Without air particles there is no one to carry the sound. In space no one can hear you scream!

sections.title: 3. The oscilloscope: pitch and volume

quizzes.question: What do you have to do on the oscilloscope to make the sound really DEEP (like a bear hum)?

answers.text: Decrease the frequency (fewer and wider waves).
answers.feedback: Richtig: Weniger Schwingungen pro Sekunde ergeben einen tieferen Ton.
Amplitude macht den Ton lauter, nicht tiefer. Die Tonhöhe hängt von der Frequenz ab.

sections.content:
Scientists want to see sound waves! To do this they use a microphone computer called Oscilloscope. He paints the invisible sound waves as jagged lines (wave crests and troughs) on a screen.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Frequency & Amplitude
- Frequency (pitch): How many times does the wave oscillate per second? When it oscillates very quickly (lots of tight waves), the sound high is like a mouse beeping. If it swings slowly, the sound deep is like the growling of a bear. This is measured in Hertz (Hz) (with a frequency meter).
- Amplitude (volume): How strong does the wave oscillate? If the wave crests are huge, the sound is loud. If they are tiny flat, the sound is quiet whispering. This is measured in decibels (dB) (with a sound level meter).

sections.title: 4. Speed ​​of Sound: The Great Race

quizzes.question: You see the lightning and count exactly 6 seconds until it thunders. How far away is the thunderstorm?

answers.feedback: 6 Sekunden sind nicht 6 km. Für 1 km braucht Schall ungefähr 3 Sekunden.
Richtig: 6 Sekunden durch 3 ergibt 2 km.

sections.content:
Sound is fast, but light is the absolute lightning champion! Light travels around the entire earth almost 8 times in one second. Sound “only” travels 340 meters per second in air. That's why we always see the lightning first in a thunderstorm and only seconds later the thunder cracks in our ears!

📖 Expect the thunderstorm trick:
Since sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 kilometer, you can do the math: count the seconds between lightning and thunder. Divide the number by 3. The result is the distance of the thunderstorm in kilometers! (If you count 9 seconds: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 kilometers away).

sections.title: 5. The Echo: Sound bounces off!

quizzes.question: How does a bat find its prey at night?

answers.text: She has huge eyes that glow in the dark like flashlights.
answers.feedback: Nicht die Augen sind entscheidend. Sie sendet Schall aus und hört auf das Echo.

answers.text: She emits ultrasound and listens for the echo that bounces off the insect.
answers.feedback: Genau: Echoortung funktioniert mit ausgesendetem Ultraschall und zurückkommendem Echo.

sections.content:
Do you remember how light particles bounce off a mirror like bouncy balls? Sound waves do that too! When you shout loudly in the mountains, the sound waves fly out, hit the hard rock wall and come back to you. This is what we call Echo (reflection of sound).

📖 Animals with superpowers: Echo sounder
Bats hunt in the dark. They shout very high (ultrasound, so high that we humans can't hear it). The sound bounces off a tiny mosquito and returns an echo. The bat's ear calculates quickly: Aha, the echo comes from the right and was there quickly - the mosquito is close! This is called Echoortung (or echo sounder for submarines).

sections.title: 6. Resonance: When sounds destroy things!

quizzes.question: Why is the thick wooden case on a guitar important?

answers.text: It's just so you can hold the guitar better.
answers.feedback: Der Kasten ist nicht nur Griff. Er schwingt mit und macht den Ton lauter.

answers.text: It is a resonance body and amplifies the quiet sound of the strings.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Der Resonanzkörper verstärkt die Schwingung der Saite.

sections.content:
Have you ever seen an opera singer make a glass shatter with just her voice? This is not a trick! Everything in the world has its own “favorite vibration” (natural frequency). If a sound hits exactly this frequency, the object suddenly begins to vibrate wildly. This resonance is called Resonance.

📖 The guitar case (sound box)
A guitar string alone sounds very quiet. But it is stretched over a large wooden box (the guitar). The string forces the wood and the air in the box to vibrate in the same rhythm. This resonance body makes the sound loud and powerful!

🍷 The Singing Glass

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "Weil Planeten den Schall verschlucken." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Weil es keine Luftteilchen (kein Medium) gibt, die den Schall weitertragen.

answers.text: Because there are no air particles (no medium) to carry the sound.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Weil es keine Luftteilchen (kein Medium) gibt, die den Schall weitertragen.

questions.question: 4. What is the name of the device that scientists use to make sound waves visible as jagged lines on a screen?

questions.question: 5. What describes the “frequency” of a sound wave?

answers.text: The number of vibrations per second (determines the pitch).

answers.text: How wide the sound wave is.

questions.question: 6. In what unit is the frequency measured?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "In Metern pro Sekunde." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: In Hertz (Hz).
Richtig: In Hertz (Hz).

questions.question: 7. You have a sound wave with a very high amplitude (huge wave crests). How does that sound?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "Sehr leise flüsternd." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Sehr laut!
Richtig: Sehr laut!

questions.question: 8. A bird peeps in a very high-pitched voice. What does this mean for the sound wave?

answers.text: It has a very high frequency.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Sie hat eine sehr hohe Frequenz.
Typischer Denkfehler: "Sie hat eine niedrige Frequenz." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Sie hat eine sehr hohe Frequenz.

questions.question: 9. Which is faster: light or sound?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "Schall ist viel schneller." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Licht ist viel schneller (deshalb kommt erst der Blitz, dann der Donner).

answers.text: Light is much faster (that's why lightning comes first, then thunder).
answers.feedback: Richtig: Licht ist viel schneller (deshalb kommt erst der Blitz, dann der Donner).

questions.question: 10. You shout "Hello!" towards a large rock face. and shortly afterwards you hear "Hello!" back. What do you call this throwing back?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "Brechung." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Echo (Reflexion von Schall).
Richtig: Echo (Reflexion von Schall).

questions.question: 11. Which animal uses extremely high ultrasound echoes to catch mosquitoes at night?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Die Fledermaus.

questions.question: 12. What is the name given to the technique in which animals (or submarines) emit sound and listen for the echo to find obstacles?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Echolot / Echoortung.
Typischer Denkfehler: "Radar-Scanner." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Echolot / Echoortung.

questions.question: 13. If a sound hits exactly the "favorite vibration" (natural frequency) of a glass, the glass begins to shake strongly. What is this effect called?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Resonanz.

answers.feedback: Richtig: Resonanzkörper.

questions.question: 15. What vibrates in our larynx when we sing or speak?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: "Unser Zäpfchen im Rachen." passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Unsere Stimmbänder.
Richtig: Unsere Stimmbänder.

arbeit.title: Mechanical work: force, distance, energy
arbeit.subtitle: Mechanical work occurs when a force acts in the direction of movement and transfers energy.

sections.title: 1. Work or just effort?

quizzes.question: You push against a thick tree with full force for 10 minutes, but it doesn't move an inch. How much physical work have you done?

answers.feedback: Nicht ganz: Wenn sich nichts bewegt, ist der Weg 0. Dann ist auch die Arbeit W = F · s gleich 0 J.
Genau: Ohne Weg keine Arbeit. Die Wand bleibt stehen, also ist W = 0 J.

sections.content:
This is what you will learn in this chapter:
  • Distinguish between everyday work and physical work.
  • use the formula W = F · s safely.
  • detect whether force and path point in the same direction.
  • Calculate work in joules.
  • Detect lifting work, friction work, deformation work and acceleration work.

In everyday life, work is anything that is stressful. In physics this is more strict: Mechanical work is only done when a force moves a body and the force points at least partially in the direction of the way.

Merksatz: Mechanical work requires power and path in the appropriate direction. Without a path, s = 0. If the force and path point crosswise to each other, the work in the direction of movement is very small or zero.

Work or no work?

sections.title: 2. Lifting work: Lift something upwards

quizzes.question: What happens to the object's energy when you do lifting work on it?

Hier geht es ums Anheben, nicht ums schneller Werden. Dabei nimmt vor allem die Lageenergie zu.

sections.content:
When you lift something upwards against gravity, you are doing lifting work. This gives the item Lageenergie.

W = m · g · h

Simplified for schools: g ≈ 10 N/kg. This means: 1 kg requires around 10 N of weight.

sections.content:
With friction work, kinetic energy or muscle work is often converted into heat. That's why hands get warm when you rub them together.

sections.title: 4. Golden Rule of Mechanics

quizzes.question: What is the Golden Rule of Mechanics?

answers.text: What you save in energy you have to use in distance.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Die Goldene Regel der Mechanik – kleine Kraft bedeutet meist längerer Weg.

answers.text: If you work a lot, you have to eat a lot.
answers.feedback: Das ist alltagssprachlich gemeint, aber nicht die physikalische Regel. In der Mechanik gilt: Kraft sparen bedeutet mehr Weg.

sections.content:
Simple machines such as ramps, levers or pulleys can save energy. But they don't magic away the work. The following usually applies: Whatever you save in energy, you have to add in distance.

sections.title: 5. Deformation work and acceleration work

quizzes.question: You step on the accelerator and your car speeds up. What work does the engine do?

answers.feedback: Genau: Das Auto wird schneller, also wird Beschleunigungsarbeit verrichtet.
Hubarbeit ist Heben gegen die Schwerkraft. Beim Beschleunigen auf gerader Strecke ist es Beschleunigungsarbeit.

sections.content:
Mechanical work can store energy or change motion. A spring stores deformation energy. A bicycle gets more motion energy.

when accelerating

Deformation work: Spring

The spring is relaxed. Hardly any deformation energy is stored.

Acceleration work: Bicycle

Increase speed. The kinetic energy increases sharply: twice the speed means approximately four times the kinetic energy.

Acceleration work: The faster the bike becomes, the greater the kinetic energy becomes. Twice as fast means about four times as much kinetic energy.

questions.question: 1. What has to happen for physics to speak of “work”?

answers.text: A force must act along a path.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Eine Kraft muss entlang eines Weges wirken.

answers.text: You just have to sweat a lot.
answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Man muss nur sehr viel schwitzen.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Eine Kraft muss entlang eines Weges wirken.

questions.question: 2. What is the formula for mechanical work?

answers.text: Work = force times distance (W = F s)
answers.feedback: Richtig: Arbeit = Kraft mal Weg (W = F · s)

questions.question: 3. In what unit is work measured?

answers.feedback: Richtig: In Joule (J).
Typischer Denkfehler: „In Newton (N).“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: In Joule (J).

questions.question: 4. You hold a 10 kg bag of flour for an hour. How much work do you do physically?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Sehr viel Hubarbeit.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: 0 Joule, weil der Weg s = 0 ist.
Richtig: 0 Joule, weil der Weg s = 0 ist.

questions.question: 5. If you carry a case of water to the second floor, it's called...

answers.feedback: Richtig: Hubarbeit.
Typischer Denkfehler: „Reibungsarbeit.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Hubarbeit.

questions.question: 6. A rocket starts and gets faster and faster. What work is being done here?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Verformungsarbeit.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Beschleunigungsarbeit (und Hubarbeit).
Richtig: Beschleunigungsarbeit (und Hubarbeit).

questions.question: 7. A car brakes sharply. The tires squeak and get hot. What work was at work?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Reibungsarbeit.
Typischer Denkfehler: „Hubarbeit.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Reibungsarbeit.

questions.question: 8. You stretch a trampoline by jumping on it. The trampoline stretches. That is...

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Reibungsarbeit.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Verformungsarbeit.
Richtig: Verformungsarbeit.

questions.question: 9. The Golden Rule of Mechanics says: "Whatever energy you save..."

answers.feedback: Richtig: "...muss man an Weg zusetzen."
Typischer Denkfehler: „"...kann man als Energie behalten."“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: "...muss man an Weg zusetzen."

questions.question: 10. A pulley will help you lift a heavy piano more easily. Does this mean you do less work overall?

answers.text: Yes, the pulley just destroys the work.
answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Ja, der Flaschenzug vernichtet die Arbeit einfach.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Nein, die Arbeit bleibt gleich, weil der Zugweg am Seil länger wird.

answers.text: No, the work remains the same because the pulling distance on the rope becomes longer.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Nein, die Arbeit bleibt gleich, weil der Zugweg am Seil länger wird.

astronomie.title: 🌌 The astrophysics adventure 🚀
astronomie.subtitle: Hello space explorers! Buckle up. We leave Earth and travel to black holes, exploding stars and the boundaries of space and time!

sections.title: 1. Cosmic dimensions: How small are we really?

quizzes.question: What unit of measurement do astronomers often use for distances in our solar system?

answers.feedback: Fast: Für riesige Strecken im All ist Millimeter viel zu klein. Zwischen Erde und Sonne nutzt man die Astronomische Einheit.
Genau. Die Astronomische Einheit (AE) ist die typische Entfernung Erde–Sonne und praktisch für unser Sonnensystem.

sections.content:
On Earth, a mountain seems huge to us. But in space, the Earth is just a tiny speck of dust. When we look into space, we have to get used to completely new dimensions. Jupiter is so big that Earth would fit over 1,300 times. And our sun? A gigantic fireball!

📖 The smart space dictionary:
Because kilometers in space are far too small numbers, astronomers measure in Astronomical Units (AU). 1 AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun (about 150 million kilometers).

sections.title: 2. The speed of light: The absolute speed limit

quizzes.question: What exactly is a "light year"?

answers.text: The time it takes to fly to the sun.
answers.feedback: Nicht ganz: Ein Lichtjahr beschreibt keine Zeit für eine Reise, sondern eine Strecke.

answers.text: The distance that light travels in a year.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Ein Lichtjahr ist die Strecke, die Licht in einem Jahr zurücklegt.

sections.content:
Nothing in the universe is faster than light. It races through space at an incredible 300,000 kilometers per second! When you turn on a flashlight, the light is on the wall almost immediately. But space is so huge that even extremely fast light takes time.

📖 The Light Year:
A light year is not a time, but a distance! It is the distance that light travels in a whole year (almost 9.5 trillion kilometers).

sections.title: 3. Gravity: When mass bends space

quizzes.question: Why is a black hole called "black"?

answers.text: Because its gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
answers.feedback: Sehr gut. Ein Schwarzes Loch wirkt schwarz, weil selbst Licht seiner extremen Schwerkraft nicht entkommt.

answers.text: Because it is made of dark charcoal.
answers.feedback: Das ist ein Mythos. Schwarze Löcher bestehen nicht aus Kohle, sondern sind Regionen mit extrem starker Gravitation.

sections.content:
Why don't we fall off the earth? Because of gravity (gravity)! Albert Einstein discovered that every heavy body (like a kind of bowling ball on a trampoline) bends the space around it. The heavier something is, the stronger it attracts other things.

📖 The Black Hole:
When a giant star dies, it can collapse. It becomes infinitely small but retains its enormous mass. Gravity becomes so extreme there that not even light can escape - a black hole is born!

sections.title: 4. Escape Velocity: Off to Space!

quizzes.question: What does a rocket have to achieve in order to leave Earth permanently?

answers.feedback: Richtig. Um die Erde zu verlassen, braucht eine Rakete etwa 11,2 km/s Fluchtgeschwindigkeit.
Zu hoch gedacht: Für das Verlassen der Erde reicht die Fluchtgeschwindigkeit, nicht die Lichtgeschwindigkeit.

sections.content:
Gravity holds us down. If a rocket wants to fly into space, it has to be incredibly fast in order to escape the Earth's gravitational pull. This speed is called escape speed. For Earth it is approximately 11.2 kilometers per second (approx. 40,000 km/h!).

📖 The rocket equation:
To go that fast you need a lot of fuel. But fuel is heavy! The more fuel you pack, the heavier the rocket becomes and the more thrust you need. A nasty cycle!

sections.title: 5. Supernova: The spectacular death of a star

quizzes.question: What happens during a supernova?

answers.feedback: Nicht ganz: Eine Supernova ist keine Kollision zweier Planeten.

answers.text: A huge star explodes at the end of its life.
answers.feedback: Genau. Eine Supernova ist die gewaltige Explosion eines massereichen Sterns am Lebensende.

sections.content:
Stars don't live forever. Inside they burn hydrogen to helium (nuclear fusion). This makes them glow. But at some point you run out of fuel! With very massive stars, gravity suddenly wins: the star collapses and hits its own core. The result? The most powerful explosion in the universe: A supernova!

drehundstatik.title: 🎡 Statics & Lever: Understanding Balance ⚖️
drehundstatik.subtitle: Why does something tip over? Why does a door open easier with the handle? Here you examine the center of gravity, torque and balance like in a small physics laboratory.

sections.title: 1. Focus: When does something tip?

quizzes.question: When is a body safe?

answers.text: When the center of gravity is above the standing surface.
answers.feedback: Genau. Solange die Wirkungslinie der Gewichtskraft in der Standfläche liegt, kippt der Körper nicht.

answers.text: If it is as colorful as possible.
answers.feedback: Die Farbe hat keinen Einfluss auf die Kippstabilität.

answers.text: If it is as high and narrow as possible.
answers.feedback: Hoch und schmal macht meist instabil, weil der Schwerpunkt leichter außerhalb der Standfläche landet.

sections.content:
This is what you will learn in this topic:
  • detect when a body is stable or tilts.
  • Explain the center of gravity, base, pivot point and lever arm.
  • predict where to press to make something spin more easily.
  • Describe circular motion and angular momentum in everyday situations.

Every body has a center of gravity. You can think of it as the point where gravity pulls. As long as the center of gravity is above the standing surface, a body stands securely.

Merksatz: Center of gravity over base = stable. Center of gravity outside the standing area = tilts.

sections.title: 3. Types of equilibrium: stable, unstable, indifferent

sections.title: 4. Circular movement: Why the carousel pulls outwards

quizzes.question: Why do the seats feel pushed outwards on the fast carousel?

answers.feedback: Genau. Wegen Trägheit will der Körper tangential weiter, die Kreisbewegung erzeugt das Gefühl nach außen.

quizzes.question: Why does a figure skater spin faster when she pulls her arms up?

answers.feedback: Richtig. Kleineres Trägheitsmoment bei gleichem Drehimpuls bedeutet höhere Winkelgeschwindigkeit.

answers.text: The arms then create a motor.
answers.feedback: Die Arme sind kein Motor; die Beschleunigung kommt aus Impulserhaltung.
Der Luftwiderstand bremst eher, statt anzuschieben.

sections.content:
When rotating, it is important how far the mass is from the axis of rotation. Arms out: slower. Arms close to the body: faster.

questions.question: What is the focus?

answers.text: The imaginary point at which the gravity of a body pulls.
answers.feedback: Genau. Der Schwerpunkt ist der Punkt, an dem man die Gewichtskraft zusammenfassen kann.

answers.text: The loudest point on a body.
answers.feedback: Nicht ganz. Es geht nicht um Lautstärke, sondern um den Punkt der Gewichtskraft.

questions.question: When does a body tip slightly?

answers.text: If the center of gravity is outside the standing area.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Liegt der Schwerpunkt außerhalb der Standfläche, entsteht ein Kippmoment.
Fast. Nur auf dem Boden zu stehen reicht nicht – entscheidend ist die Lage des Schwerpunkts.

questions.question: What does a wide footprint do?

answers.text: It makes a body more stable.
answers.feedback: Ja. Eine größere Standfläche macht Kippen schwieriger und erhöht die Stabilität.
Nein. Die Standfläche ändert nicht automatisch die Masse, sondern vor allem die Kippstabilität.

questions.question: What is the pivot point on a door?

answers.feedback: Genau. Das Scharnier ist die Achse, um die sich die Tür dreht.
Nicht korrekt. Die Farbe ist egal; Drehpunkt ist das Scharnier.

questions.question: Where is the easiest place to push open a door?

answers.text: On the handle, far away from the hinge.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Weit vom Scharnier ist der Hebelarm groß, daher braucht man weniger Kraft.
Fast. Nahe am Scharnier ist der Hebelarm klein, deshalb ist mehr Kraft nötig.

questions.question: What is a lever arm?

answers.text: The distance from the pivot point to the acting force.
answers.feedback: Genau. Der Hebelarm ist der Abstand zwischen Drehpunkt und Angriffspunkt der Kraft.
Nicht ganz. 'Hebelarm' ist kein Körperteil, sondern ein geometrischer Abstand.

questions.question: What creates a large torque?

answers.text: From strength and a long lever arm.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Großes Drehmoment entsteht durch große Kraft und/oder großen Hebelarm.

answers.text: With little distance and no strength.
answers.feedback: Nein. Mit kleinem Abstand und kaum Kraft entsteht nur ein kleines Drehmoment.

questions.question: What does stable equilibrium mean?

answers.text: After a nudge, the body returns.
answers.feedback: Genau. Beim stabilen Gleichgewicht kehrt der Körper nach einer kleinen Störung zurück.

answers.text: After a nudge it will surely fall away.
answers.feedback: Nicht korrekt. Wegkippen nach kleinem Stups beschreibt kein stabiles Gleichgewicht.

questions.question: What does unstable equilibrium mean?

answers.text: A small nudge can cause the body to tip over.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Beim labilen Gleichgewicht reicht ein kleiner Impuls, damit der Körper kippt.
Nein. 'Besonders sicher' wäre eher stabiles Gleichgewicht, nicht labiles.

questions.question: What does indifferent equilibrium mean?

answers.text: The body remains in the new location after moving.
answers.feedback: Genau. Beim indifferenten Gleichgewicht bleibt der Körper in der neuen Lage.

answers.text: The body is getting faster and faster.
answers.feedback: Nicht ganz. Es geht nicht um schneller werden, sondern um Lage ohne Rückstellwirkung.

questions.question: Why do you feel pushed outwards on the fast-moving carousel?

answers.text: Your body wants to keep going straight because of its inertia.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Wegen der Trägheit will dein Körper seine geradlinige Bewegung beibehalten.
Nein. Das Gefühl kommt nicht durch Magnetismus, sondern durch Trägheit im rotierenden System.

questions.question: What keeps you going in circles on the carousel?

answers.text: A force towards the center, for example chain or seat.
answers.feedback: Genau. Für Kreisbewegung braucht es eine nach innen gerichtete Kraft (Zentripetalkraft).

answers.text: An invisible engine in the body.
answers.feedback: Nicht korrekt. Kein 'Körpermotor' hält die Bahn; es ist die Kraft zur Mitte.

questions.question: What happens during a pirouette when the arms are pulled up?

answers.feedback: Richtig. Arme anziehen verringert das Trägheitsmoment, dadurch steigt die Drehgeschwindigkeit.
Nein. Die Drehung stoppt nicht sofort; meist wird sie sogar schneller.

questions.question: Where is the mass when the arms are outstretched?

answers.text: Further away from the axis of rotation.
answers.feedback: Genau. Mit ausgestreckten Armen ist mehr Masse weiter außen, das Trägheitsmoment wird größer.
Nicht korrekt. Die Masse liegt dann nicht nur im Fuß, sondern weiter weg von der Achse.

questions.question: Which terms belong to leverage?

answers.text: Pivot point, force, load and lever arm.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Das sind die zentralen Hebelbegriffe für Berechnung und Verständnis.
Nein. Temperatur, Farbe und Lautstärke gehören nicht zur Hebellehre.

elektrizitaet.title: ⚡ The electricity adventure ⚡
elektrizitaet.subtitle:
Hello! Nice that you're here. Here you will learn step by step how electricity works.
        Read the explanations carefully, look at the pictures, do the small exercises and test your knowledge in the quizzes.
        You collect points for every correct action! Have fun!

sections.title: 1. The invisible particles (charges)

quizzes.question: An electron (-) and a proton (+) meet:

answers.feedback: Richtig: Plus und Minus ziehen sich an.
Gleiche Ladungen stoßen sich ab. Plus und Minus ziehen sich an.

quizzes.question: 1. Which particles are negatively charged and can move easily?

answers.feedback: Protonen sitzen im Atomkern und bewegen sich im Kabel nicht frei.
Ganze Atome wandern im Kupferdraht nicht als Strom durch das Kabel.
Richtig: Elektronen können sich in Metallen leicht bewegen.

sections.content:
Everything around us consists of tiny building blocks called atoms. Smaller particles that have an electric charge live in these atoms. Think of them like little charged balls.

An atom: The heavy, positive nucleus in the middle and the fast, negative electrons around the outside.

  • 🔴 Protons: These are positively (+) charged. They are heavy, sit firmly in the atomic nucleus and almost never move.
  • 🔵 Electrons: These are negatively (-) charged. They are tiny and absolute whirlwinds. They zip around the core on tracks!

The most important rule of electricity is:
Same things don't like each other (repel each other). But opposites attract!

The basic rule: like charges want to move away from each other, unlike charges want to move towards each other.

{{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s0_q0}} {{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s0_q1}}

sections.title: 2. What is electricity actually?

quizzes.question: A piece of rubber (e.g. an eraser):

answers.feedback: Richtig: Gummi lässt Strom kaum durch.
Gummi ist ein Isolator. Metall wäre ein Leiter.

quizzes.question: 1. Why is the outside of your phone charger cable made of plastic?

answers.text: Because plastic is an insulator. It prevents us from getting electrocuted.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Plastik schützt dich, weil es Strom schlecht leitet.

answers.text: Because it looks nicer and feels better.
answers.feedback: Aussehen ist nebensächlich. Plastik ist außen, weil es isoliert.

sections.content:
Imagine a river with water flowing in it. Electric current is exactly the same - except that instead of water flowing, billions of small, negative electrons (-).

So current is just: Moving electrons, all rushing in the same direction through a cable.

Like water in a pipe: many small electrons flow together through the cable.

In order for them to flow, they need a path (a cable). But be careful, not every material lets electrons through!

  • 🟢 Leader: These are materials in which the electrons can slide freely like on a slide. (Examples: copper, iron, gold, water).
  • 🔴 Isolators: These are "electron prisons". They hold the electrons tight, nothing can flow. (Examples: plastic, rubber, wood, glass).
{{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s1_q0}} {{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s1_q1}}

sections.title: 3. Circuit & Resistance

quizzes.question: You're building a circuit, but a wire in the middle is cut (the wire ends don't touch). What happens?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Der Kreis ist offen, also bleibt die Lampe aus.
Bei einer Lücke gibt es keinen geschlossenen Weg. Die Lampe kann nicht leuchten.

quizzes.question: 1. What happens when current flows through a wire with very high resistance?

answers.feedback: Ein Draht friert durch Strom nicht ein. Hoher Widerstand wandelt Energie in Wärme um.

answers.text: The wire slows down the electrons and becomes warm in the process.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Widerstand bremst den Strom und der Draht wird warm.

quizzes.question: In which circuit do all the other lamps continue to shine if one lamp breaks?

answers.text: In parallel connection (each has its own path)
answers.feedback: Richtig: In der Parallelschaltung hat jede Lampe einen eigenen Weg.

answers.text: In series connection (like on a string)
answers.feedback: Bei der Reihenschaltung ist eine kaputte Lampe wie eine Lücke im ganzen Kreis.

sections.content:
For a lamp to light, the electrons must be able to flow in a circle. They start at the battery, flow through the lamp and have to come back to the battery. This is called a closed circuit.

Types of circuits:

  • The series connection: All lamps (or components) hang one after the other on the same cable like pearls on a string. Attention: If a lamp breaks, the circuit is broken and all the others go out too! (E.g. with old fairy lights).
  • The parallel connection: The cable branches! Each lamp has its own little extra path to electricity. Advantage: If one lamp breaks, the others continue to burn happily. This is also how the sockets in your apartment are wired.

A closed circuit: the current can flow in a circle.

The current brake (resistor): Even in a super conductor (like copper) the electrons do not flow completely freely. The material slows it down a bit. A thin cable brakes more than a thick cable. When the electrons have to squeeze through a thin cable, they rub against each other and the cable gets hot. That's exactly how a toaster works!

{{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s2_q0}} {{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s2_q1}} {{QUIZ_elek_q_parallel}}

sections.title: 4. The battery: The power pump

quizzes.question: What is the name of the part in the battery that blocks the direct path for the electrons?

answers.feedback: Die Kathode ist der Pluspol. Der Elektrolyt trennt innen die Ladungen.
Richtig: Der Elektrolyt verhindert den direkten Kurzweg in der Batterie.

quizzes.question: 1. Where do the electrons start their journey through the circuit?

answers.text: At the negative pole (anode) because there are too many electrons there.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Elektronen starten am Minuspol.
Elektronen sind negativ. Sie werden vom Pluspol angezogen, starten aber am Minuspol.

sections.content:
Electrons are a bit lazy. They don't just flow out on their own. They need a “nudge”. This push is called electric voltage. A battery is like a pump that creates this push.

The inside of a battery: Chemistry creates the charge difference.

  • 🔴 The anode (negative pole): Lots of free electrons are created here through chemistry. So it's extremely crowded here!
  • 🟢 The cathode (positive pole): There is a shortage of electrons here. The electrons really want to get over here.
  • 🔵 The electrolyte: This is a thick paste in the middle. He's like a wall! The electrons can't just fly directly inside. You must take the long detour outside through the cable (and through our lamp)!
{{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s3_q0}} {{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s3_q1}}

sections.title: 5. The capacitor: The energy storage

quizzes.question: 1. What is special about a capacitor compared to a battery?

answers.text: It delivers consistent power over many hours.
answers.feedback: Eine Batterie liefert länger gleichmäßig Strom. Ein Kondensator gibt kurz und schnell Energie ab.

answers.text: It can release energy very quickly at once (e.g. for lightning).
answers.feedback: Richtig: Kondensatoren können Energie sehr schnell freigeben.

sections.content:
A capacitor stores energy, but differently than a battery. It works more like a taut arch or a dam.

It consists of two metal plates that do not touch each other. There is an insulator in between (e.g. air). When we pump electricity into it, the electrons accumulate on one plate. You want to get to the other, positive plate, but the insulator is blocking the way! The tension rises.

A charged capacitor: the charges are opposite each other, separated by the insulator.

The energy is now stored. The highlight: If you connect the capacitor to a flashlight lamp, for example, it can release all of the stored energy in a flash!

{{QUIZ_elektrizitaet_s4_q0}}

sections.title: 6. Ohm's Law: U, I and R

quizzes.question: What happens to the current (I) if you increase the voltage (U) but the resistance stays the same?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Mehr Spannung schiebt bei gleichem Widerstand mehr Strom.
Bei gleichem Widerstand macht mehr Spannung nicht weniger Strom.

sections.content:
How are voltage, current and resistance related? The physicist Georg Simon Ohm has found the answer! He discovered Ohm's law. It's like a three-way relationship:

  • Voltage (U) in volts (measuring device: voltmeter): The pressure that pushes the electrons.
  • Current intensity (I) in amperes (measuring device: ammeter): How many electrons flow through per second.
  • Resistance (R) in ohms (measuring device: ohmmeter): How strongly the wire slows down the electrons.

The formula is: U = R · I (voltage = resistance times current). This means: More pressure (U) creates more current (I)! A high resistance (R) makes less current (I).

sections.title: 1. Ørsted's discovery: Electricity makes magnets

quizzes.question: What happens around a cable when current flows?

answers.text: A circular magnetic field is created.
answers.feedback: Genau. Um den Leiter liegen kreisförmige Feldlinien. Merksatz: Strom erzeugt Magnetfeld.
Wärme kann auch entstehen, aber die Kernidee hier ist das Magnetfeld um den Draht.

sections.content:
People used to think that electricity and magnets had nothing to do with each other. But in 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass needle moves when you hold it next to a wire carrying current.

📖 The clever word: field lines
We draw the invisible field as lines. In the case of wire, there are concentric circles around the conductor.

sections.content:

sections.title: 3. The Relay: The magnetic switch

quizzes.question: Why do you use relays?

Relais können indirekt sparen, ihr Hauptzweck ist aber sicheres Schalten und galvanische Trennung.

sections.content:
A Relay is a switch that is operated with an electromagnet. When current flows through the control coil, it pulls a metal lever (armature), completing another circuit.

quizzes.question: What does an electric motor convert electrical energy into?

sections.content:
Moving charges (current) in the magnetic field sense a force: the Lorentz force. In a motor, this force is used to rotate a coil in a circle.

answers.text: By moving a magnet in a coil.

sections.title: 6. The transformer: voltage change

quizzes.question: Why does a transformer only work with alternating current?

answers.text: Because direct current is too weak for the iron core.
answers.feedback: Der Kern ist nicht das Problem. Bei Gleichstrom fehlt die laufende Feldänderung für Induktion.

answers.text: Because the magnetic field must constantly change to induce current in the second coil.
answers.feedback: Genau. Nur ein veränderliches Magnetfeld induziert in der zweiten Spule eine Spannung.

sections.content:
A transformer consists of two separate coils on a common Iron core. He uses the mutual induction:

  • The Primary coil uses alternating current to generate a constantly changing magnetic field.
  • The iron core passes this magnetic flux to the second coil.
  • This induces a new voltage in the secondary coil.

questions.question: Who discovered electromagnetism in 1820?

answers.feedback: Newton war wichtig für Mechanik. Elektromagnetismus wurde 1820 von Ørsted beobachtet.
Stimmt: Ørsted zeigte 1820 den Zusammenhang zwischen Strom und Magnetismus.

questions.question: What happens around every current-carrying conductor?

answers.feedback: Genau: Ein Magnetfeld entsteht um jeden stromdurchflossenen Leiter.

questions.question: What do you call a coiled roll of wire?

answers.feedback: Ein Kondensator speichert Ladung, ist aber keine aufgewickelte Drahtrolle.

questions.question: What material is best suited as a core for an electromagnet?

answers.feedback: Aluminium ist leitfähig, aber als Kern für starke Elektromagnete ungeeignet.
Genau. Eisen/Weicheisen ist als Kernmaterial besonders wirksam.

questions.question: What happens to the magnetic force when you wind more turns on a coil?

answers.feedback: Umgekehrt: Mehr Windungen verstärken die Feldwirkung der Spule.

questions.question: What is the force on moving charges in a magnetic field called?

answers.feedback: Ja. Das ist genau das Prinzip eines Elektromagneten.

questions.question: Which device converts electrical energy into motion?

answers.feedback: Ein Relais ist kein Spannungswandler. Es ist ein magnetisch betätigter Schalter.

questions.question: What is the principle of a bicycle dynamo?

answers.feedback: Schwerkraft wirkt auf Masse, nicht spezifisch auf Ladungen im Magnetfeld.
Richtig. Lorentzkraft wirkt auf bewegte Ladungen im Magnetfeld.

questions.question: What has to change for current to be induced in a coil?

answers.feedback: Genau. Dreht sich der Stromfluss, dreht sich auch die Kraftrichtung.

energie.title: ⚡ The energy adventure 🔋
energie.subtitle: Hello energy tamers! Get ready, we're exploring the invisible force that drives our universe!

sections.title: 1. What is energy? The invisible engine!

quizzes.question: What unit is energy measured in?

answers.feedback: Kilogramm misst Masse. Energie messen wir in Joule.
Richtig: Joule ist die Einheit der Energie.

sections.content:
Imagine you are lying lazily on the sofa. To get up and run into the next room, you need something specific: Energy! Energy is the ability to move, heat, or make things glow. You can't touch it or weigh it, but you can see what it does. Without energy absolutely nothing would happen in the entire universe - everything would stand still!

📖 The smart dictionary: Joule
Just like you measure distance in meters, you measure energy in Joules (J) (pronounced like "Juul"). To lift an apple (approx. 100 grams) one meter high, you need around 1 joule of energy!

🏋️ The dumbbell experiment (positional and kinetic energy)

Lift the dumbbell to "store" its energy (positional energy/potential energy). Drop them to convert the energy into movement (Kinetic Energy)!

The dumbbell is on the floor. No energy stored.

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. The big magic trick: energy conversion

quizzes.question: What does the law of conservation of energy say?

answers.text: Energy cannot disappear, it only transforms into other forms.
answers.feedback: Genau: Energie verschwindet nicht. Sie taucht in anderer Form wieder auf.

answers.text: You can create energy out of nothing if you put in the effort.
answers.feedback: Aus dem Nichts kommt keine Energie. Sie wird nur umgewandelt.

sections.content:
Now comes the most important thing you need to know about energy: Energy can never be created or destroyed! It only ever changes from one form to another. This is called the law of conservation of energy. When a light bulb lights up, electrical energy is converted into light energy (and heat). Nothing is lost!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Forms of Energy
There are many "costumes" for energy:
- Motion Energy (A rolling car)
- Lageenergie (A stone on a mountain)
- Heat energy (A hot heater)
- Electrical energy (electricity in the socket)

⏱️ The Tireless Pendulum

Click "Nudge". Watch how the pendulum has positional energy at its highest point, which turns into motion energy as it falls!

Pendulum rests.

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Chemical energy: The power snack

quizzes.question: What form of energy is in an apple you eat?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Im Essen ist chemische Energie gespeichert.
Elektrische Energie steckt zum Beispiel in einem Stromkreis, nicht direkt im Apfel.

sections.content:
Where do YOU ​​actually get your energy to run and play? From your food! There is chemical energy in foods such as apples, bread or pasta. Your body works like a small engine: it burns this chemical energy and uses it to generate kinetic energy and body heat. There is also chemical energy in batteries and car gasoline!

📖 Calories = Energy!
You often see the word “calories” (kcal) on food packaging. This is just another unit for energy (1 kcal = approx. 4184 joules). The more calories, the more energy there is in the food!

🔋 The Hungry Flashlight

Insert the battery to convert the chemical energy into electrical energy and then into light energy!

Flashlight is off. Energy is missing!

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Where does our electricity come from? Renewable energy

quizzes.question: Why are wind power and solar energy called “renewable” energies?

answers.text: Because you can buy them new in the supermarket.
answers.feedback: Erneuerbar heißt nicht: neu kaufen. Wind, Sonne und Wasser liefern immer wieder Energie.

answers.text: Because they are never used up and are available indefinitely.
answers.feedback: Genau: Diese Quellen werden durch Nutzung nicht einfach aufgebraucht.

sections.content:
In order to operate our televisions, cell phones and lamps, we need an extremely large amount of electrical energy. In the past, coal or oil was burned for this purpose (fossil energies). The problem: This creates bad air (CO2) and at some point the coal runs out. Today we are using more and more renewable energies! We use the power of wind, sun and water. This energy never runs out and doesn't make any mess!

💨 The wind power plant

Move the slider to make the wind blow stronger. The faster the wheel spins, the more electricity (energy) is generated!

Wind strength: 0% (calm)

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. The circuit: On the electron highway

quizzes.question: Why does a lamp not light when the cable is cut?

answers.text: Because the circuit is broken and the electrons can no longer flow.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Ohne geschlossenen Kreis fließt kein Strom.

answers.text: Because the electrical energy evaporates in the cable.
answers.feedback: Energie verdampft nicht im Kabel. Der Weg für die Elektronen ist unterbrochen.

sections.content:
For electrical energy to work, it needs a closed path - the circuit. Electricity consists of tiny particles (electrons) that zip through copper cables. But be careful: they only flow when the circle is completely closed, like on a car racing track! If the cable is broken or a switch is open, all electrons stop immediately and the device switches off.

💡 The light switch

The switch is open (the circuit is broken). Click on it to close the circuit!

Circuit is interrupted. The lamp is off.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

questions.question: 1. What is “energy” simply explained?

answers.text: An invisible gas in the air.
answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Ein unsichtbares Gas in der Luft.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Die Fähigkeit, etwas zu bewegen, zu wärmen oder leuchten zu lassen.

answers.text: The ability to move, warm or make something glow.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Die Fähigkeit, etwas zu bewegen, zu wärmen oder leuchten zu lassen.

questions.question: 2. In what unit do physicists measure energy?

answers.feedback: Richtig: In Joule (J).
Typischer Denkfehler: „In Grad Celsius (°C).“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: In Joule (J).

questions.question: 3. What happens according to the “law of conservation of energy”?

answers.text: Energy disappears into thin air over time.
answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Energie löst sich mit der Zeit in Luft auf.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Energie geht nie verloren, sie wandelt sich nur in andere Formen um.

answers.text: Energy is never lost, it just transforms into other forms.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Energie geht nie verloren, sie wandelt sich nur in andere Formen um.

questions.question: 4. If you pick up a stone and hold it, what energy does it have?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Elektrische Energie.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Lageenergie (Potenzielle Energie).
Richtig: Lageenergie (Potenzielle Energie).

questions.question: 5. If you let go of the stone and it falls, what does the positional energy turn into?

answers.feedback: Richtig: In Bewegungsenergie (Kinetische Energie).
Typischer Denkfehler: „In chemische Energie.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: In Bewegungsenergie (Kinetische Energie).

questions.question: 6. Where is “chemical energy” located?

answers.feedback: Richtig: In Lebensmitteln, Benzin und Batterien.
Typischer Denkfehler: „In einem Spiegel.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: In Lebensmitteln, Benzin und Batterien.

questions.question: 7. A toaster gets hot when you turn it on. What transformation is taking place?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Bewegungsenergie wird zu chemischer Energie.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Elektrische Energie wird zu Wärmeenergie.
Richtig: Elektrische Energie wird zu Wärmeenergie.

questions.question: 8. Which is NOT a renewable energy source?

answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Wind und Sonnenlicht.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Kohle und Erdöl.
Richtig: Kohle und Erdöl.

questions.question: 9. What happens in a wind power plant?

answers.text: The kinetic energy of the wind is converted into electrical energy.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Die Bewegungsenergie des Windes wird in elektrische Energie verwandelt.

answers.text: Electrical energy is used to make wind (like a fan).
answers.feedback: Common mix-up: electricity does not create the wind here. The turbine converts the wind's motion energy into electrical energy.

questions.question: 10. What must be present for electricity from a battery to light a lamp?

answers.text: The lamp must be larger than the battery.
answers.feedback: Typischer Denkfehler: „Die Lampe muss größer sein als die Batterie.“ passt hier nicht. Korrekt ist: Der Stromkreis muss vollständig geschlossen sein.

answers.text: The circuit must be completely closed.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Der Stromkreis muss vollständig geschlossen sein.

farben.title: 🌈 The secret of colors 🎨
farben.subtitle: Why is the sky blue and a rose red? Everything starts in the atoms and with tiny waves. Let's solve the puzzle of colors together!

sections.title: 1. How light is born in the atom

quizzes.question: What happens when an electron falls back into its comfortable, inner orbit?

answers.feedback: Licht verschwindet nicht einfach: Eine Lampe erzeugt und sendet Licht aus, das sich ausbreitet.
Genau: Eine Lichtquelle sendet Licht aus, das dann auf Gegenstände trifft.

sections.content:
Do you remember the electrons? When you give atoms energy (e.g. through heat or electricity), the electrons become very fidgety. They make a quantum leap to a higher orbit. But they can't stay there!

📖 The clever word: photons
When an electron falls back from its high orbit, it has to get rid of the energy. It spits out a tiny packet of energy: a Photon. This is the light we see!

Electron falls back = light packet (photon) is released!

{{QUIZ_farben_s1_q0}}

sections.title: 2. Wavelengths: The “size” of the color

quizzes.question: Which color of light has the shortest waves and therefore the most energy?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Ein blauer Pullover reflektiert vor allem blaues Licht in dein Auge.
Nicht ganz: Rot wird eher geschluckt. Der Pullover wirkt blau, weil vor allem Blau reflektiert wird.

sections.content:
Light moves in waves, just like water waves in the ocean. The distance between two wave crests is the wavelength. And it is exactly this length that determines which color we see!

🌊 The wave scanner

Select a wavelength:

Select a button above!

🔴 Red: Has the longest waves.
🔵 Blue: Has the shortest waves (lots of energy!).
{{QUIZ_farben_s2_q0}}

sections.title: 3. The Prism: The Rainbow Trick

quizzes.question: What color is hidden in white sunlight?

answers.feedback: Fast: Gelb ist nur ein Teil. Sonnenlicht enthält viele Farben – zusammen als weißes Licht.
Genau: Weißes Sonnenlicht besteht aus vielen Farben, die man im Spektrum sehen kann.

sections.content:
White light (from the sun) is actually a mixture of ALL colors! When white light flows through a glass triangle (prism), the colors are "refracted" to different degrees and are arranged next to each other.

A prism separates white light into its colorful components.

{{QUIZ_farben_s3_q0}}

questions.question: 1. What is spat out of the atom when light is produced?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Ein Photon ist ein kleines Licht-Paket.
Nein: Atome spucken keine Dinge aus. Bei Licht entsteht ein Photon.

questions.question: 2. What is the wavelength of blue light compared to red light?

answers.feedback: Genau: Blaues Licht hat kürzere Wellen als rotes Licht.
Nicht richtig: Längere Wellen passen eher zu rotem Licht.

questions.question: 3. Where do the colors of the rainbow in the sky come from?

answers.text: Water drops act like small prisms and refract sunlight.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Tropfen brechen Sonnenlicht und trennen die Farben.

answers.text: The sun paints the colors with an invisible brush.
answers.feedback: Nein: Die Farben entstehen durch Brechung, nicht durch Malen.

questions.question: 4. What do you call the jump of an electron to a higher orbit?

answers.feedback: Genau: Der Sprung auf eine andere Bahn heißt Quantensprung.
Fast im Alltag, aber physikalisch heißt es Quantensprung.

questions.question: 5. What color is the lowest energy light?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Rotes Licht hat die niedrigste Energie im sichtbaren Licht.
Nicht ganz: Blaues Licht hat mehr Energie als rotes Licht.

questions.question: 6. What happens in a prism with white light?

answers.text: It is broken down into spectral colors.
answers.feedback: Genau: Ein Prisma zerlegt weißes Licht in Spektralfarben.
Nein: Das Prisma schluckt das Licht nicht, es trennt die Farben.

questions.question: 7. Which color is refracted the most?

answers.feedback: Nicht richtig: Rot wird am wenigsten stark gebrochen.
Richtig: Violett und Blau werden stärker abgelenkt als Rot.

questions.question: 8. What is wavelength?

answers.feedback: Genau: Wellenlänge ist der Abstand von Berg zu Berg.
Nicht ganz: Die Wellenhöhe ist nicht die Wellenlänge.

questions.question: 9. Why is a leaf green?

answers.text: It reflects green light and absorbs the rest.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Das Blatt wirft grünes Licht zurück ins Auge.
Nein: Ein Blatt leuchtet nicht selbst. Es reflektiert grünes Licht.

questions.question: 10. What is light physically?

answers.feedback: Nein: Licht ist kein Stoff, den man anfassen kann.
Richtig: Licht ist eine elektromagnetische Welle.

questions.question: 11. What happens when all colors are mixed (light)?

answers.feedback: Genau: Gemischtes farbiges Licht kann weißes Licht ergeben.
Nicht richtig: Schwarzes Licht entsteht nicht durch das Mischen von Lichtfarben.

questions.question: 12. Which device breaks up light like a rainbow?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Ein Prisma zerlegt Licht wie beim Regenbogen.
Nein: Ein Hammer kann Licht nicht in Spektralfarben zerlegen.

questions.question: 13. How fast is light approximately?

answers.feedback: Zu langsam: Licht ist viel schneller als 100 km pro Stunde.
Richtig: Licht bewegt sich ungefähr 300.000 km pro Sekunde.

questions.question: 14. What does an electron need to jump to an external orbit?

answers.feedback: Nein: Ein Elektron braucht Energie, keinen Keks.
Genau: Mit Energie kann ein Elektron auf eine äußere Bahn springen.

questions.question: 15. What color is the sun really (outside the atmosphere)?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Außerhalb der Atmosphäre erscheint die Sonne weiß.
Nicht ganz: Gelb wirkt sie oft durch die Erdatmosphäre.

kraft_und_bewegung.title: 🚀 Strength & Movement: Newton in everyday life ⚡
kraft_und_bewegung.subtitle: Why do you fly forward when braking? Why does ice slip better than carpet? Here you learn powers with your body, images and short experiments.

sections.title: 1. What is a force?

quizzes.question: How do you know that a force is working?

answers.text: Something starts, stops, speeds up, slows down, changes direction or deforms.
answers.feedback: Correct: You can recognize force by a change in motion or shape.
Noise can occur, but it is not reliable proof of force.

answers.text: Just because something has a color.
answers.feedback: Color does not show force. Look for motion, braking, direction, or shape changes.

sections.content:
You can do this after this chapter:
  • Recognize and name forces in everyday life.
  • explain why things don't start or stop by themselves.
  • Explain friction, gravity, recoil and lever with examples.
  • use the formula F = m · a in simple words.

A force is a push, a pull or a push. You don't see a force directly. You recognize them by their effect: Something moves, brakes, changes direction or is deformed.

Note: A force can change the state of motion of a body. In physics, force is abbreviated F and measured in Newton (N). The measuring device is called Kraftmesser.
Mini-assignment: Look around the classroom. Where is the pull, push, brake or hold happening? Give three examples.
{{QUIZ_q_force_intro}}

sections.title: 2. Inertia: Things want to stay that way

quizzes.question: Why does a soccer ball on the grass stop at some point, but an asteroid in space continues to fly for a very long time?

answers.text: Friction and air resistance slow things down on the grass. In space there is almost nothing that slows you down.
answers.feedback: Exactly: friction and air resistance slow the ball down.
Objects do not get tired. A force must slow them down.

answers.text: The asteroid has a built-in engine.
answers.feedback: Ohne Motor kann etwas weiterfliegen, wenn fast nichts bremst.

sections.content:
Have you ever experienced tipping forward on the bus when the bus brakes hard? Your body wanted to keep going. This is called inertia.

📖 Newton's 1st insight: A body remains at rest or continues to move smoothly as long as no force causes it to do something else.

⚽ The lazy football in space

1. Guess: What happens after the push when almost nothing brakes?

2. Test: Give the ball a push.

Thinking question: Why is a seat belt important in the car? It exerts a force on your body when you brake.
{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 3. Friction: The brake between surfaces

quizzes.question: Why do you slip better on tiles with socks than on a thick carpet?

answers.text: The carpet creates more friction and brakes more strongly.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Teppich bremst stärker durch mehr Reibung.

answers.text: Tiles are cold, and cold pulls you forward.
answers.feedback: Cold does not pull forward. What matters is friction between surfaces.
The carpet does not change your mass. It just causes stronger braking.

quizzes.question: Which friction is usually the smallest?

answers.text: Rolling friction, for example with wheels.
answers.feedback: Exactly: wheels reduce friction a lot.

answers.text: Static friction, when a heavy box doesn't even start to slip.
answers.feedback: Static friction is often large because starting motion is hard.

answers.text: Sliding friction, when something scrapes across the ground without wheels.
answers.feedback: Gleitreibung ist meist größer als Rollreibung.

sections.content:
Friction occurs when two surfaces rub against each other. Even smooth things are not entirely smooth under the magnifying glass. Small bumps get stuck. That slows you down.

Three types: Static friction is the hard start. Sliding friction brakes when sliding. Rolling friction is usually the smallest, which is why wheels help.

🧊 The slide race: ice against carpet

1. Guess: Which block will move further with the same force?

Black ice: little friction

Carpet: lots of friction

📦 The cabinet transport

Which method saves energy?

{{QUIZ_q2}} {{QUIZ_q_friction_types}}

sections.title: 4. Gravity: The earth pulls

quizzes.question: What happens if you drop a hammer and a feather on the moon at the same time?

answers.text: Both fall at the same speed because there is practically no air resistance.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Ohne Luftwiderstand fallen beide gleich schnell.

answers.text: The hammer falls faster because it is heavier.
answers.feedback: That sounds logical, but on the Moon the braking air is missing.

answers.text: The feather stops in the air.
answers.feedback: The feather does not stay still. It is also pulled by the Moon's gravity.

sections.content:
The earth attracts everything: you, your table, a ball and also the air. We call this attraction Gravity or Gravitation.

📖 Mass and weight: Your mass stays the same everywhere. Your weight depends on how hard a planet or moon pulls on you. On the moon your weight is much smaller.

🍎 Apple and feather

1. Guess: What happens without air?

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 5. Action and Reaction: Forces come in pairs

quizzes.question: You inflate a balloon and let it go. Why is he flying away?

answers.text: Air shoots out the back. As a counterforce, the balloon flies forward.
answers.feedback: Genau: Luft nach hinten, Ballon nach vorne.
Mass does not suddenly become larger. This is about equal and opposite force.

answers.text: The balloon automatically searches the sky.
answers.feedback: Der Ballon hat kein Ziel. Die herausströmende Luft drückt ihn weg.

sections.content:
When you push something, it pushes back. Always. Equally strong, but in the other direction. This is called action and reaction.

Merksatz: Force and counterforce belong together. Example: You push the wall. The wall pushes you back.

🚀 The rocket launch

Observe: Which direction are the gases going? Which direction is the rocket going?

Partner assignment: Two people stand on roller boards or non-slip socks on a smooth floor and press their hands against each other. What happens? Only try it out with a teacher and at a safe distance.
{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 6. Force, mass, acceleration: F = m · a

quizzes.question: What happens if the same force is applied to a much heavier object?

answers.feedback: Correct: the same force gives less acceleration when mass is larger.
Heavier objects react more slowly with the same force, not faster.
Mass does not disappear. More mass makes acceleration harder.

sections.content:
An empty shopping cart is easy to push. A full shopping cart requires more strength. This is exactly what Newton's 2nd law describes.

F = m a

  • F means power. Unit: Newton (N).
  • m means mass. Unit: Kilogram (kg).
  • a means acceleration: getting faster, braking or changing direction.

🧪 The F = m · a laboratory

Change power and mass. The acceleration is calculated immediately.

Acceleration: 2.0 m/s²

More power makes you faster. More mass makes you slower.

🎥 Animation: Adding forces

If two forces act at the same time, you can add them together as arrows.

{{QUIZ_q_newton2}}

sections.title: 7. Lever: Save energy with travel

quizzes.question: What helps if you want to lift a heavy stone with a crowbar?

answers.text: Press far back so that the lever arm is long.
answers.feedback: Correct: a longer effort arm saves force.

answers.text: Press very close to the stone.
answers.feedback: Very close to the stone, the effort arm is short. Then you need a lot of force.
Eine kürzere Stange macht den Hebel schlechter.

sections.content:
A lever is a rod with a pivot point. This allows you to move heavy things with less force. To do this you have to press a longer way.

📖 Lever law simple: Long power arm means: You need less strength. Short power arm means: you need more strength.

⚖️ The seesaw construction site

1. Guess: Where does the blue pivot point have to go so that the little red weight can lift the heavy load?

2. Test: Move the blue pivot point. Goal: The heavy load should go up.

Pivot point position: Center

Power arm: medium
Distance from pivot point to red weight.
Load arm: medium
Distance from pivot point to heavy load.

Chance to lift the load:

Both arms are similar in length. The heavy load wins.

Everyday check: Search lever: door handle, scissors, pliers, nutcracker, seesaw. Mentally mark three points: pivot point, force, load.
{{QUIZ_q5}}

questions.question: What is a force?

answers.text: A push, pull, or pressure that can change motion or shape.
answers.feedback: Correct: a force can change motion or shape.
No: color is a property, not a force.

questions.question: What does inertia mean?

answers.text: Things remain at rest or continue to move until a force acts.
answers.feedback: Exactly: without a new force, rest or motion stays as it is.

answers.text: Things always want to stop automatically.
answers.feedback: Not quite: objects stop only when a braking force acts.

questions.question: Why does a bicycle eventually stop rolling?

answers.text: Friction and air resistance slow down.
answers.feedback: Correct: friction and air resistance remove motion from the bicycle.
No: mass stays the same. Friction and air slow the bicycle.

questions.question: Which friction is usually the best when transporting?

answers.feedback: Exactly: rolling is usually easier than sliding or starting.
Not exactly: static friction is strongest at the start, not during steady transport.

questions.question: What pulls you back to the ground after a jump?

answers.feedback: Richtig: Die Schwerkraft zieht dich zur Erde zurück.
No: floor color does not pull you downward.

questions.question: What stays the same on the moon: mass or weight?

answers.feedback: Genau: Deine Masse bleibt gleich, auch auf dem Mond.
Not correct: weight becomes smaller on the Moon.

questions.question: Why do hammers and springs fall at the same speed in a vacuum?

answers.text: Without air resistance, both accelerate equally.
answers.feedback: Correct: without air, the feather is not slowed more strongly.
No: they do not become equally heavy. The braking effect of air is missing.

questions.question: What does action and reaction mean?

answers.text: For every force there is an equal counterforce in the other direction.
answers.feedback: Exactly: every force has an equal opposite force.
No: music is irrelevant. This is about action and reaction forces.

questions.question: Why does a rocket fly up?

answers.text: It pushes gases downwards, the opposing force pushes them upwards.
answers.feedback: Richtig: Gase nach unten bedeuten Gegenkraft nach oben.

answers.text: She pulls herself up on stars.
answers.feedback: No: stars do not pull the rocket upward. The exhaust gases push it.

questions.question: What does F = m · a simply say?

answers.text: More mass requires more force for the same acceleration.
answers.feedback: Exactly: more mass needs more force for the same acceleration.

answers.text: Strength has nothing to do with mass.
answers.feedback: Not correct: force, mass, and acceleration are linked.

questions.question: What is acceleration?

answers.text: Speed ​​up, slow down or change direction.
answers.feedback: Correct: acceleration means any change in speed or direction.
No: loudness is not acceleration.

questions.question: How do you measure strength?

answers.feedback: Exactly: force is measured with a force meter in newtons.

answers.text: With a thermometer in degrees Celsius.
answers.feedback: Not correct: a thermometer measures temperature, not force.

questions.question: Why does a long lever arm help?

answers.text: You need less force, but you have to push a longer distance.
answers.feedback: Correct: a long lever saves force, but the path becomes longer.
No: a lever does not make the load disappear. It redistributes force and distance.

questions.question: Where is a lever in everyday life?

answers.feedback: Exactly: these tools work with a lever.
Nicht passend: Ein ruhendes Heft ist kein typischer Hebel.

questions.question: What do you need to shoot a rolling ball in a different direction?

answers.feedback: Correct: only a force can change the ball's direction.
No: a wish does not change motion. You need a force for that.

linsen_spiegel.title: 🌈 The optics adventure 🔦
linsen_spiegel.subtitle: Welcome, young researchers! Buckle up, we're traveling on a beam of light through the exciting world of optics!

sections.title: 1. Reflection: Ping-Pong with light

quizzes.question: What is the name of the invisible guide line that stands vertically on the surface when mirrored?

answers.feedback: Noch nicht. Der Ausfallstrahl ist der zurückgehende Lichtstrahl. Für Winkel brauchst du das Lot als senkrechte Referenz.
Genau. Das Lot ist die senkrechte Hilfslinie am Auftreffpunkt. Zu ihm misst man Einfalls- und Ausfallswinkel.

sections.content:
Light particles often behave like perfect little bouncy balls. If you throw a bouncy ball at an angle against a smooth wall, it will bounce back the same way in the other direction. The light does exactly the same thing on a smooth mirror! In physics, this reflection is called Reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Law of Reflection
To measure how obliquely the light hits the mirror, physicists paint an invisible guide line exactly perpendicular (at a 90-degree angle) onto the mirror. This line is called the Lot.
The angle between the incoming light beam and the plumb line is called Infallwinkel. The law of nature is super simple: angle of incidence = angle of reflection!

🎮 The Laser Mirror

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Refraction: The kink in optics

quizzes.question: Why does the light beam bend when it hits the water at an angle?

answers.text: Because the water is optically denser and slows down the light.
answers.feedback: Richtig. Im optisch dichteren Wasser wird Licht langsamer und ändert deshalb die Richtung.

answers.text: Because the water is wet and washes away the light.
answers.feedback: Das klingt alltagstauglich, erklärt aber die Physik nicht. Der Knick kommt durch die andere Ausbreitungsgeschwindigkeit im Medium.

sections.content:
Light is extremely fast in empty space. But when it travels through materials like water or thick panes of glass, it has to work harder and is slowed down slightly. If a beam of light enters such a material at an angle, it suddenly changes direction as it brakes. We call this Brechung!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Optical Density
Water and glass are harder to penetrate than air. They are said to have a higher optical density. Imagine running across asphalt and running diagonally into a basin full of modeling clay. The foot that first steps into the dough is immediately slowed down. The other foot continues to run quickly - this means you automatically make a curve! This is exactly how the light bends towards the plumb.

🧪 The Pelvic Laboratory

Select which material the laser beam should shine into:

Current: Air (Same density, beam just goes straight)

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Total internal reflection: When light is caught

quizzes.question: What happens to the light beam during total reflection?

answers.text: It is completely reflected back at the interface like a mirror.
answers.feedback: Genau. Bei Totalreflexion bleibt der Strahl komplett im dichten Medium und wird wie am Spiegel zurückgeworfen.
Nicht ganz. Energie geht nicht einfach weg: Der Strahl wird ab dem Grenzwinkel vollständig reflektiert.

sections.content:
Imagine you are underwater and looking diagonally up at the surface. At a certain angle something magical happens: the light can no longer leave the water! Instead, it is reflected at the surface of the water like a perfect mirror. We call this Total reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Limit Angle
Total internal reflection only happens when light moves from an optically dense substance (like water or glass) into a thinner substance (like air) - and at a very shallow angle. The angle at which this happens is called limit angle.

🔦 The light in the glass rod

Move the laser. From a certain angle the light is no longer refracted, but totally reflected!

{{QUIZ_q_total}}

sections.title: 4. The Eye: Your built-in camera

quizzes.question: What does the lens of the eye do to help us see things close up clearly?

answers.text: It becomes thicker and more curved.
answers.feedback: Perfekt. Für nahe Objekte wird die Linse stärker gekrümmt und damit brechkräftiger.
Das gilt für Fernsicht. Für Nähe braucht das Auge eine dickere, stärker gekrümmte Linse.

sections.content:
Your eye works almost like a digital camera. There is a lens at the front that focuses the light and projects a sharp image onto the back wall of the eye (the retina). The crazy thing: Everything on the retina is upside down! Your brain only turns the image the right way around again.

Two types of lenses:

  • Converging lens (convex lens): It is thicker in the middle than at the edge (curved outwards). It focuses the light into one point (focal point). The magnifying glass is a typical collecting lens!
  • Diffusing lens (concave lens): It is thinner in the middle than at the edge (curved inwards, like a "cave"). It scatters the rays of light outwards as if they were flying apart.

Memory tip: Convex curves outward (like a belly). Concave curves inward (like a cave).

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Accommodation
So that you can clearly see both the cell phone right in front of your nose and the distant church tower, your eye can deform the lens. Muscles flatten them (for distance) or make them thick (for close). This trick is called accommodation.

👁️ The vision simulator

Your eye adapts: click on the objects to see how the lens deforms!

Choose a distance!

{{QUIZ_q_auge}}

sections.title: 5. Lenses: light bundlers and diffusers

quizzes.question: Which lens do you use if you want to concentrate the sun's light in one point like with a magnifying glass?

answers.feedback: Ja. Eine Konvexlinse bündelt paralleles Licht im Brennpunkt, wie bei einer Lupe.
Fast. Eine Konkavlinse streut Licht nach außen und kann es nicht in einem echten Brennpunkt sammeln.

sections.content:
We use refraction by shaping glass into precise curved forms. These pieces of glass are called lenses. They are used in magnifiers, glasses, and cameras.

📖 Two shapes, two tricks:
- Collecting lens (convex lens): It is nice and thick and bulbous in the middle. It captures light rays and directs them inward until they all meet in one super-hot spot: the focal point (focus).
- Diffusing lens (concave lens): It is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It pushes the rays outwards as if they were being scattered.

💡 Memory tip: Convex = curved outwards. Concave = curved inwards (like a cave).

🔍 The lens changer

Click to replace the lens:

Converging lens (convex): Focuses all rays at the focal point!

sections.title: 4. Diffraction: Light goes around the corner!

quizzes.question: When does light bend most strongly into new circular waves?

answers.text: When the gap is extremely narrow.
answers.feedback: Genau. Ein enger Spalt erzeugt starke Beugung: hinter dem Spalt breitet sich das Licht seitlich aus.

answers.text: When the gap is open like a giant barn door.
answers.feedback: Umgekehrt: Bei großem Spalt bleibt der Strahl fast gerade. Starke Beugung sieht man bei kleinem Spalt.

sections.content:
We previously thought that light rays only travel stubbornly straight ahead. But surprise: light actually behaves like a wave in the ocean! When this light wave hits an extremely tiny obstacle or a very narrow gap, it shows its magical nature.

📖 The clever dictionary: The diffraction (Huygens' idea)
The scientist Christiaan Huygens discovered the Huygens principle. He said: Every tiny point of a light wave can create a whole new spherical wave! If a gap is extremely narrow, we force the light through there. Suddenly the tiny gap looks like its own little lamp, and the light spreads out in a circle behind it. This is called Diffraction.

🌊 The diffraction lab

Click on the box to gradually narrow the gap:

Wide slit: The light passes through almost exclusively as a straight wave (wave front).

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. Curved Mirrors: The Funhouse Cabinet

quizzes.question: Which outwardly curved mirror is often hanging at dangerous street intersections because it allows you to see a very wide field?

answers.feedback: Das wäre der bündelnde Spiegel. Für breites Sichtfeld an Kreuzungen braucht man den nach außen gewölbten Konvexspiegel.
Richtig. Konvexspiegel geben ein großes Sichtfeld, daher nutzt man sie an Kreuzungen und in Märkten.

sections.content:
Thick glass lenses are often quite heavy! Sometimes we simply use curved mirrors made of metal. They behave surprisingly similarly to our lenses.

📖 The mirror-lens twin:
- Hollow mirror (concave mirror): Light falls into the recess like a soup spoon. It behaves like a converging lens! It focuses the light in front of it into a real focal point.
- Wölbspiegel (convex mirror): The light hits the round "belly" (like a Christmas tree ball). It behaves like a diverging lens. The light fans out and creates a virtual focal point for our eyes that appears to be behind the mirror!

🪞 The Mirror Cabinet

Click to flip the mirror:

Hollow mirror (concave): Focuses the light like a converging lens.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. The microscope: journey to the smallest animals

quizzes.question: How many lenses does a simple microscope need at least?

answers.feedback: Genau. Ein einfaches Mikroskop arbeitet mit Objektiv und Okular.
Nicht ganz. Eine einzelne Linse ist eher eine Lupe. Für ein Mikroskop braucht man mindestens zwei Linsen.

sections.content:
To observe bacteria or cells, we place two lenses in a long tube. The lower lens near the specimen is the objective. The upper lens near the eye is the eyepiece.

📖 The Invisible Image:
The lens collects the light from the tiny sample and projects an upside-down, enlarged Intermediate image floating freely in the middle of the tube. The eyepiece now acts like a powerful magnifying glass that we point at this floating image. If the intermediate image is exactly in the violet focal point of the eyepiece, the image in the eye becomes razor-sharp!

👁️ View through the eyepiece

Out of focus!

💡 Focus tip: First adjust controller 1 until the gray intermediate image lies well in the tube. Then slide controller 2 until the purple focus point exactly touches the intermediate image!
{{QUIZ_linsen_s6_q0}}

sections.title: 7. The telescope: look at the stars

quizzes.question: What two parts does the famous Newton telescope (reflector) use to direct light into our eyes?

answers.text: A large primary mirror and a small secondary mirror.
answers.feedback: Correct. In a Newton telescope, the primary mirror collects the light and the secondary mirror redirects it to the eyepiece.

answers.text: A concave lens and a convex lens.
answers.feedback: Das beschreibt ein Linsensystem. Das Newton-Teleskop ist ein Reflektor mit zwei Spiegeln.

sections.content:
A telescope for astronomers doesn't have to have an incredibly high magnification. More importantly, it collects as much faint starlight as possible! For this you need a telescope with a huge aperture.

📖 Why mirrors win over lenses:
The classic refracting telescope (we call it Refractor) uses glass lenses. But gigantic lenses weigh tons! The glass is flattened under its own weight and the image deforms. In addition, thick lenses create ugly color errors (rainbow edges) at the edges.
That's why Isaac Newton built the first mirror telescope (reflector). At the very back of the tube there is a huge, curved main mirror made of metal. It focuses the light forward, where a small, slanted secondary mirror throws the light sideways into the eyepiece. Perfect for giant observatories!
